heard: A single day on Mercury outlasts two of its entire years. Astronomers long believed the planet was tidally locked, matching an 88-day orbit with an 88-day spin. Under that permanent lock, one roasted hemisphere reached extreme temperatures exceeding 700 Kelvin. In 1965, scientists bounced radar beams off Mercury to measure its actual spin rate from Earth. Italian celestial mechanics specialist Giuseppe Colombo propose the planet actually rotates once every 59 Earth days. Mercury is not locked one-to-one, but instead rotates three times for every two orbits around the Sun. Because orbital motion combines with that spin, a single solar day lasts approximately 176 Earth days. Every morning, there takes two full planetary years to arrive.
